blocks.text: It is proved that עכשוב achsub is the asp.

The question is what עכשוב achsub is in these words of Psal. CXL, 4: חמת עכשוב תחת שפתימו, The poison of achsub is under their lips. The Chaldee renders it אורסא דעכוביתא, the poison of the spider, as though עכשוב were, κατ᾽ ἀναγραμματισμὸν [kat᾽ anagrammatismon], the same as עכביש. The Arabic translator has سم الافاعي [samm al-afāʿī], the poison of vipers. Others have the poison of the asp; I rather agree with these, because, besides the Greek translators, the Latin, the Syriac, Apollinaris and Jerome, and among the Hebrews Kimchi, Mardochaeus and Pomarius, they also have Paul the Apostle on their side, who renders the words of the Psalmist thus in Roman. III, 13.: Ἰὸς ἀσπίδων ὑπὸ τὰ χείλη αὐτῶν [Ios aspidōn hypo ta cheilē autōn]. It might seem that עכשוב achsub alludes to the word עכס eches, which some explain as the poison of a serpent, others as a species of viper. The former is asserted by R. Selomo on Esa. III, 16. in these words: עכס הוא ארס של נחש, Eches is the poison of a serpent. The latter by the author of the Mechilta, and from him Aquinas: עכס הוא מין אפעה שכשרואה העוף פורח באויר יתחבר אל צלו ואיבריו נושרין וזהו צלמות צל ועמו מות, Eches is a species of viper which, when it sees a bird flying, joins itself to its shadow, and its feathers fall off; and this is the shadow of death, or the deadly shadow. But both are mistaken. For עכס eches is nothing other than the Greek ἔχις [echis], that is, the male viper. Nor did the Greeks borrow that word from the Hebrews, but the later Hebrews from the Greeks. Therefore whoever tries to trace עכשוב achsub, a genuinely Hebrew word, back to it is trifling.

But I think I detect its true etymology from the Arabic language, in which عكس achasa means to turn back and to bend a thing back to its starting point, whether this happens in a straight line, as in the reflection of the sun, which in Avicenna is called انعكاس [inʿikās] ^{a)}, or by circles and coils, as when a serpent, its head turned toward its tail, gathers itself into a coil. Hence Alcamus: تعكس في مشيته مشي مشيا الافعي [taʿakkasa fī mashyatihi mashā mashyan al-afʿā] He walked with the gait of a viper, that is, turning himself in a circle. Perhaps among the Hebrews עכש was the same, whence עכשוב, with the letter Beth added at the end. Just as from כרך, to go around, comes כרכוב, circuit, Exod. XXVII, 5. And from the Chaldee תעל the Arabic ثعلب [thaʿlab], fox. And ערבוב, mixture, from the verb ערב, to mix. And זרבוב, a casting-vessel, from the verb זרב, to flow. And any others of this kind. This name certainly fits the nature of the asp [col. 380] perfectly, since, as Nicander testifies ^{b)}, it is wont κατ᾽ ἐναντίον ἕρπειν [kat᾽ enantion herpein], to crawl in the contrary direction, that is, بالعكس [bi-l-ʿaks] ^{c)}. Not to mention that the same Nicander describes it fighting thus, in line 166:

[III, 155] Ὁλκῷ δὲ τροχόωσαν ἅλων᾽ εἰλίξατο γαίῃ. Σμερδαλέον δ᾽ ἀνὰ μέσσα κάρη πεφρικὸς ἀείρει· [Holkō de trochoōsan halōn᾽ eilixato gaiē. Smerdaleon d᾽ ana messa karē pephrikos aeirei] It traces winding coils with rounded trail, and thus raises its dreadful head from the middle of the circle.

So too the Etymologicum: Συστρέψαν ἑαυτὸ πολεμεῖ, καὶ μάχεται [Systrepsan heauto polemei, kai machetai]; Twisting itself together, it wages war and fights. Συστρέφειν ἑαυτὸ [Systrephein heauto] in Arabic is تعكس [taʿakkasa]. Thus in Oppian's Cynegetica book 3, line 446, the ichneumon tears apart the asp

coiled on this side and that. And in Phylarchus, whom Aelian cites in book 17, ch. 5, tame asps τὴν μὲν λοιπὴν σπεῖραν ἐῶσι κατὰ τοῦ δαπέδου, ἀρᾶσαι δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν περιλιχμῶνται [tēn men loipēn speiran eōsi kata tou dapedou, arasai de tēn kephalēn perilichmōntai], leave the rest of the coil on the ground, but with head raised they lick round about. That the same animal εἰς κύκλους πολλοὺς ἑλισσόμενον καθεύδειν [eis kyklous pollous helissomenon katheudein], sleeps coiled into many circles, is asserted by the Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Wasps. These circles are called Οἶμοι [Oimoi] in Greek. Hesychius: Οἶμον, οἶμος· ὁδὸς, κύκλος, τρίβος. ὅθεν καὶ τῆς ἀσπίδος κύκλους οἴμους ἐκάλεσαν [Oimon, oimos; hodos, kyklos, tribos. hothen kai tēs aspidos kyklous oimous ekalesan]. In Arabic you would rightly say انعكاس [inʿikās]. Accordingly the Hebrew name of the asp, עכשוב, seems to be derived from this, in the way we have said. Nor is the reason for the Greek name different. For Ἀσπὶς [Aspis] is used both for a shield and for a serpent. That the shields of the Greeks were round you may learn even from the Poet, by whom the round eye of Polyphemus is described ^{d)}:

Hence in Homer everywhere ^{e)} ἀσπίδες εὔκυκλοι [aspides eukykloi] and ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι [aspides omphaloessai], where the Scholion has στρογγύλαι, περιφερεῖς [strongylai, periphereis]. And in Diodorus ^{f)}, τὸν τῆς ἀσπίδος κύκλον μιμησάμενος [ton tēs aspidos kyklon mimēsamenos], imitating the circle of the shield. Whether the name ἀσπὶς [aspis] for the shield was derived from the serpent, as the Scholiast of Aristophanes holds, or the serpent's name from the shape of the shield, which it seems to reproduce with its coils, as the Etymologicum would have it, we do not care to investigate, since it is not relevant to our subject ^{*)}.
